abstract: The temporal organization of episodic memory is thought to depend critically on the hippocampus, potentially coordinated by theta-band oscillations. Here, we used concurrent transcranial alternating current stimulation (tACS) and functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) to examine whether slow theta stimulation (3 Hz) applied over the left parietal cortex modulates hippocampal-cortical functional connectivity during memory encoding, and how this relates to subsequent temporal memory performance. Twenty-seven participants encoded sequences of object-scene pairs that were presented either within a single context or across a context boundary, under different tACS conditions (3 Hz, 8 Hz, and no stimulation), and afterwards judged the temporal distance between item pairs. Behaviorally, 3 Hz stimulation led to significantly compressed temporal distance judgments compared to 8 Hz, suggesting altered temporal memory reconstruction. Further, 3 Hz tACS selectively reduced hippocampal connectivity with occipital cortex, comprising left calcarine and lateral occipital clusters, and reduced hippocampal activity during encoding. In contrast, 8 Hz tACS reduced connectivity between the stimulation site and right early visual cortex. Neither frequency modulated hippocampal-cortical connectivity during retrieval. These results suggest that slow theta oscillations can shape hippocampal-cortical network dynamics in a frequency-specific manner, influencing the construction of temporal relations in memory.
